en: The *Prakaraṇapañcikā*, composed by the Great Professor Śālikanātha Miśra, who bore the yoke of the tradition of the illustrious Guru Prabhākara.
The eighth treatise, titled *Tattvāloka*, adorned with the commentary named *Nyāyasiddhi* and the glosses on difficult passages (*viṣamasthala-ṭippaṇī*).
The Declaration of the Subject Matter:
746 Regarding the reality of the self (ātmatattva), 747 there are various disputes among proponents. We, the Prābhākaras, shall strive for the determination of that truth. 748 // 1 //
Thus [it is said].
However, others maintain that the sense-faculties themselves are [the self];
likewise, some assert that there is an inferable entity distinct from the cognitive faculties and the body.
Some, however, maintain that it is accessible through mental perception; others consider it established by all forms of cognition;
and some say that it is momentary.
Others say it is immutably eternal;
those who maintain that it is omnipresent and so forth dispute this. Likewise, [some say] it is one and the same in all fields (*kṣetra*).
Others maintain that it is different in each field (*kṣetra*). To determine the truth regarding this matter, the following established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is commenced.
The self is distinct from the intellect, the sense organs, and the body; it is all-pervading, eternal, and manifold, appearing in each field with respect to the cognitions of objects. // 2 //
Thus ends the objection from the perspective of the Vijñānavādins:
"But surely we do not perceive any difference between cognition and the cognizer."
How so?
Because from the cognition "I perceive the jar," cognizers apprehend a self distinct [from the cognition].
True; it is like the cognition of a double moon and the like.
The authoritative scholars maintain that this is an error, like the cognition of an object and its reflection.
Furthermore, the difference between consciousness and the cognizer is refuted by the rule of their simultaneous perception,
because difference is pervaded by the absence of such a rule [of simultaneity].
Because it is sublated by the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalambha*). As they say:
"For the nature of consciousness is indeed undivided, yet it is seen as such by those whose vision is distorted by error."
It appears as if possessing a distinction between the apprehended object, the apprehending subject, and the cognition itself.
Thus,
even those who maintain that the cognizer is distinct from cognition, they too assert that his status as a cognizer exists only when cognition itself is present with respect to its object.
And in this way, let that very [consciousness] alone be the knower; what is the use of another knower? And thus, the self (ātman) becomes the knower.
The self is indeed consciousness (*buddhi*).

It is self-luminous and flows as an beginningless continuum through the relationship of cause and effect; however, in states such as sleep, intoxication, and fainting, it does not repeatedly enter the path of reflective awareness due to being suppressed. Nevertheless, it persists even during those conditions.
Otherwise, it would follow that the arising of cognition in the waking state and so forth would be impossible.

This very beginningless stream of cognition, which is based on beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*), which perceives and determines distinctions within the conditioned, and which functions under the power of the origin [of suffering], transmigrates. However, when the origin is severed by the uprooting of all latent impressions of the view of a self (*sattvadṛṣṭi*) through the direct realization of the nature of the Path, one is liberated.
Likewise, for the Tāyins, there is the cessation of the continuum (*saṃtāna*).
As they say: "The liberation of that Tāyin is like the extinguishing of a lamp."

Thus, for the teachers, whose mental continuums are purified and who possess a great compassion— perfected through practice over many lifetimes— that pervades the entire world from Brahmā down to a blade of grass— their continuum is infinite;
this is the refutation [of the objection].
This is without substance,
because it is impossible to refute the distinction between the cognition and the cognizer, which is established by common experience;
furthermore, the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambha-niyama*) is compatible with their being distinct.
We shall explain this further in this very context;
moreover, this [position] has been refuted in the *Ṛjuvimalā* regarding the establishment of external objects.
Let consciousness alone be supreme.
As for what was said, "Enough of a knower," that too is appropriate to say regarding a conceptual knower; however,
when a knower is established through direct perception, there is no room for such idle chatter.
As for the claim that cognition persists even during sleep and other such states,
that too is baseless due to a lack of evidence.
We shall explain the cause of cognition in this very context with respect to waking and other states.
The presentation and refutation of the doctrine that the sense-faculties are the self:
"In that case, let the sense-faculties themselves be conscious;
in this way, the appearance of a distinction between the intellect (*buddhi*) and the knower will be established."
This would be so if there were no unification of a single object through seeing and touching;
for in the cognition, "That which I saw, that I now touch," a single unifier is perceived.
Furthermore, the recollection of sense-objects is observed even when those respective senses have ceased to function.
That [consciousness] is not tenable as the sentience of the sense organs.
In refuting the doubt regarding the doctrine that the body is the self:
"In that case, let the body itself be the self."
These two faults would not apply there;
but it is not so, for the self is indeed the knower.
Furthermore, the status of being a knower is not possible for the body.
For instance, what is called the "body" is a specific material substance composed of earth.
Now, if it were purely earthen, one would encounter the consequence that the qualities of other elements would not be perceived in it.
We say "no.

We maintain that one element, when conjoined with other elements, does not produce a different effect; however, we do not assert that the elements do not combine with one another even in mutual association.
Therefore, the perception of qualities belonging to other constituent elements combined with it is not untenable.
But how is it that their capacity to initiate [a new substance] is impossible?
It is said: first of all, it is not so for the five [gross elements].
Alternatively, it is not possible for four [atoms] to act as producers in combination;
for if a substance were produced by both visible and invisible substances, that which inheres in it would necessarily result in being invisible.
Indeed, whatever is produced by both visible and invisible substances, and whatever inheres therein, [would share those properties].
That [body] is not visible to the eye,
like the conjunction of wind and a tree;
yet the body is indeed visible to the eye.
Therefore, it is not initiated by five or four [elements],
because space and wind are not visible to the eye.
An Examination of the Non-Visual Nature of Space:
But how is it that space is not an object of visual perception?
Furthermore, one must also consider this: even for that which is not visually perceived, what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its existence?
It is said: space is not visible to the eye, because, while being a substance, it is formless, like the self.
[Objection: But surely the sky is not formless; for it is white.
It is observed that [the snow] is as dark as the petals of a blue lotus.
It is said: for whiteness generally belongs only to that which is luminous (taijasa), such as fire or gold.
Because that [blue color] is not perceived when that [space] is absent;
furthermore, as for this blue color which is observed at night,
it does not belong to the sky.
To whom, then, does it belong? To no one at all.
But how, then, is it a quality?
Of nothing? True.
This very quality (guṇa) is unestablished. [Objection:
But surely it is established by the force of cognition (pratīti). [Reply:
True; it would be established if cognition itself were established.
But that [perception] is not established because of the absence of its cause.
Is it not the eye itself that is the cause? No;
for the eye does not illuminate when it is independent of the assistance of light.
Therefore, this delusion of perception in those who are dull-witted occurs precisely because [the blue] is not perceived;
hence, it is not apprehended during the day.
Otherwise, the eye, assisted by the solar rays, would manifest the blueness in the sky even more clearly.
If one were to manifest it [thus],
then since form is accompanied by tangibility, space would possess tangibility.
Consequently, there would follow the undesirable consequence that all material substances possess resistance.
However, some say that the blueness of darkness is perceived just like the blueness of the sky;
others maintain that this is incorrect.
Because the production of darkness is untenable; for if darkness possessed color, it would be a substance,
and being composed of multiple substances, it would necessarily be visible to the eye.
Furthermore, those substances do not exist;
if they did exist, they would be perceived even during the day.
Therefore, it is logical that this conceit of blueness belongs to the sky itself, just as it does for the blind.
The dispelling of darkness.
As for that which is said— "Shadow itself is darkness, and it is a real entity possessing qualities such as mobility and immobility, largeness and smallness, distance and proximity"—
and as for that mobility, immobility, and so forth which have been set forth; [these are untenable].
That too is due to superficial observation;
for instance, when light is obstructed, a shadow is perceived.
Yet, apart from the existence of the ground or other locations where the light has been obstructed, no shadow is seen as a distinct entity, like some other form of color.
Therefore, we consider that "shadow" (*chāyā*) is simply a portion of space and so forth from which light has been excluded.
By this, [the properties of] mobility and immobility, largeness and smallness, distance and proximity, and so on, are established.
Let there be a substance that obstructs light; [yet it is not the shadow itself].
In whatever manner it moves, in that very manner light is released and obstructed.
The shadow appears as if it were moving;
otherwise, while the body moves, why would the shadow also move?
By this, the immobility [of the shadow] when the body is immobile is explained.
Greatness consists in possessing number and dimension;
in the absence of that, how could this shadow possibly arise? Enough, then, with this talk from one who sees only the gross and lacks connection to the truth.
Objection: If shadow is merely a portion of the earth or the like, how can it be designated by a separate substance as "this is the shadow of that"?
Response: It has been stated that shadow is simply a portion of the earth or the like from which light is excluded. In that case, that by which the exclusion occurs—
In relation to that [shadow], such a designation is appropriate;
and in this way, the conventional usage of the authors of the Smṛtis—such as "one should not intentionally step upon a shadow"—is also logically established.

Furthermore, as for the convention used by the authors of the treatises—namely, that "the effect characterized as shadow is the same for umbrellas, houses, and so forth"—this is to be explained with the intention of referring to the exclusion of light.
[Objection: But if there were an exclusion of light, would it not follow that the ground and other such things could not be seen?
[Reply: Not so.
In that case, the conjunction of a greater number of light-particles is what is excluded;
however, a few particles of light, moving from all sides, do indeed come into conjunction.
But where there is a total absence of their conjunction, [darkness is perceived].
It is faultless to say that [the sky] is a great darkness.
As for the claim that one with wide-open eyes perceives the void situated within the water in wells and the like,
the response is that even there, particles of light, delimited by the rim of the well, are perceived in that manner.
There is a suspicion that space is not established;
yet, this being the case, it is not that space is unestablished,
because it is established through inference from the quality characterized by sound.
But surely, the status of sound as a quality (*guṇa*) is unestablished, since it is accepted by the proponents [of its reality] as being a substance (*dravya*).
As they say: "And those sounds whose nature consists of phonemes (*varṇa*) are eternal and likewise all-pervading."
However, because they are not separate substances, they are not considered qualities belonging to anything.

[The opponent claims: "As stated in the *Sāṃkhyadarśanakośa*, page 92: 'That [claim] is refuted because, by being perceived by a single sense organ, its status as a quality (*guṇatva*) is established, just like color and so forth.'"
Nor is there the fallacy of inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva) due to air,
because that air is admitted to be beyond the reach of the senses (atīndriya);
and even for those who maintain that air is perceptible by the senses, [the same applies].
There is no fault in this case either, because of the inclusion of the qualification "when there is an absence of contact.
Thus, sound, having its status as a quality established, will lead to the inference of a substratum (guṇin).
Since there is no cause for it to be understood as being of the nature of earth, water, and so forth, it remains as a distinct substance (dravya) altogether.
Because difference is understood through the distinction between the quality of unperceived co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and difference itself.
[Objection: But surely the word is perceived as residing in the face and so forth.
[Reply: No, it is said.
The auditory faculty functions by reaching its object because it is an external sense organ, like the tactile faculty.
In this regard, the auditory faculty does not first travel to the location of the mouth or other such places,
for the ear-drum is directly perceived as remaining in its own place.
Nor does the mouth approach the location of the ear, since that too is perceived only in its own location;
therefore, it is the sound as it has reached the ear that is apprehended.

This notion that "the word is in the mouth" is indeed an error; for it is not possible for sound, being a subordinate factor, to have an acquisition characterized by conjunction. Its acquisition must therefore be characterized solely by inherence (*samavāya*).

And thus, since the auditory organ has sound as its quality, it is established that the substance characterized by the quality of sound— which is denoted by the term "space" (ākāśa)— is itself the auditory organ.
Now, it might be argued that the ear is the ear-cavity, which is composed of earth, and that one perceives sound residing in space through the relation of inherence in what is conjoined;
but this is not so.
For when direct attainment is possible, it is not logical to resort to an indirect process.
Nor can the body be composed of all three [elements], because that would entail the manifestation of other qualities;
for earth, water, and fire possess, respectively, the sensations of touch that are neither hot nor cold, cold, and hot.
The substance initiated by those [atoms] would come to possess a touch distinct from these three [qualities], like a variegated cloth;
just as a cloth initiated by white, black, and other threads possesses a color distinct from the colors of the threads themselves.
Likewise, the body would also have a touch distinct from the touch of its constituent substances;
yet this [body] is perceived as having a touch that is neither hot nor cold.
By this, its dual nature is also refuted.
Furthermore, since it is impossible for a single odor inherent in an earthly substance to originate another odor, the body would be odorless.
Moreover, if water and fire, or fire and water, were the originating causes, the body would likewise lack odor.
Thus, its lack of taste should be understood.
Therefore, a body possessing color, taste, odor, and tangibility is composed of earth alone; and consciousness belongs to the specific quality [of the self].

Furthermore, in an effect-substance (*kāryadravya*), a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) is necessarily preceded by the qualities of its causes, just like color (*rūpa*) and so forth. However, cognition does not exist in the earth-atoms (*pārthivaparamāṇu*) which serve as the causes; for it is not observed in other substances such as jars (*ghaṭa*) that are composed of them.
The removal of doubt according to the Cārvāka school:
It might be argued that consciousness is like the power of intoxication.

For instance, just as the power of intoxication arises in the atoms of earth even though it is not present in the resulting effect-substance called wine which is composed of them, [so too might consciousness arise].
"In that case, consciousness too will be produced.
That is not so, because power is not a non-specific quality (aviśeṣaguṇa).
For the quality called *śakti* (potency) is accepted as existing in all substances, pertaining to their respective effects and being cognizable through those effects; however,
since consciousness does not exist elsewhere than in the body and so forth,
it is a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*).

Moreover, due to conjunction with other substances, even in earth-atoms which have not yet become an effect, the quality called "intoxicating power" (*mada-śakti*) is not untenable, even though it does not arise from the qualities of its [own] causes.
In the resulting substance called wine, which is produced by those atoms, it arises precisely from the qualities of its causes.
However, consciousness (*caitanya*) is not admitted to exist in each individual atom.
Therefore, since knowledge is a quality belonging to something other than the body,
this should be understood as an inference for a person distinct from the body.
This concludes the presentation of the doubt and its refutation according to the view of the Vijñānavādins.
It might be thought: "The quality-status (*guṇatva*) of cognition itself is unestablished.

This is because it must reside in a substance (*dravyāśritatvāt*), and because its status as a quality is established by the absence of being an independent cause with respect to conjunction and disjunction due to its being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatayā*).
Nor should it be said that the very fact of being dependent on a substance (*dravyāśritatva*) is unestablished; for [the self] is an effect (*kārya*).
Indeed, no effect whatsoever acquires its own nature without depending on a substance.
In this same way, it should be understood that from pleasure and so forth, there is an inference of a person distinct from the body.
Furthermore, the objection based on the support of the notion of "I" (ahaṅkāra) regarding the doctrine that the body is the self is not valid. Why is this so?

Because in the cognition "I know the jar," the knower is the locus of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), and because there is no dispute regarding the application of the ego-sense to the body alone in such instances as "I go" or "I am stout," it is the body itself that is perceived as the knower through direct perception;
and when there is a contradiction with direct perception, inference finds no footing for itself.
Even if knowledge were a specific quality (*vaiśeṣikaguṇa*), it would not be preceded by qualities in its cause;
thus, although knowledge does not exist in the atoms of earth, it might still arise in the body.
Therefore, there is no inference [of a self] other than the body.
Objection: If consciousness belongs to the body, then it should also exist in a dead body. No;
because that [dead body] is devoid of its essential qualities.
It is undisputed that the body becomes devoid of its qualities through death.
[Objection: Surely the notion of "I" (ahaṅkāra) is applied to something distinct from the body, as in the thought, "This is my body.
[Reply: No; even though there is no actual difference, this is a figurative application of distinction, just as in the expression, "the body of the stone statue" (*śilāputrakasya śarīram*).
Otherwise, because of the designation "my self" (*mamātmā*), one would have to postulate yet another self.
Furthermore, those [qualities] such as pleasure and so forth,

being understood as related to the object of the ego-notion (*ahaṃkāra*)— as in “I am happy”— are inherent in the body alone; therefore, they are not capable of inferring a self that is distinct from it.

Furthermore, because they are the cause of modifications in the body, they are all the more clearly qualities of the body; for that which is not a quality of something cannot possibly effect a modification in that substratum.
For the body undergoes transformation through the dilation of the eyes, the brightening of the face, the bristling of the hair, and so forth,

when pleasure and other sensations arise; since the body is the substrate cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) with respect to that transformation, it is logical that its non-substrate cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) should also be something closely connected to it.
Nor can it be argued that the conjunction of the self with that which possesses pleasure and so forth is itself the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) for the modifications inherent in the body;
for there is a lack of evidence (*pramāṇābhāva*).
Indeed, this hypothesis could only be maintained if the self were already established.
However, since it is appropriate that only those factors immediately preceding the probandum (sādhya) possess causality,
pleasure and other such qualities lack the capacity [to prove] the inference of a self distinct from the body.
This is their refutation.
To this it is replied: This might be so if no knower were perceived as distinct from the body.
In the cognition "I perceive the jar," the perceiver of the jar appears to be distinct from the body;
for the body is that which possesses limbs such as hands and feet.
Furthermore, at the time of the experience of a jar or other objects, its manifestation does not persist [as a common factor].
And it must necessarily be accepted that the manifestation of the knower persists throughout the experiences of the objects of cognition;
otherwise, there would follow the absurd consequence that there is no distinction between what is cognized by oneself and what is cognized by another.
Even at the time of acting with the thought, "I am going," the agent—who is essentially distinct from the body—is indeed perceived as the goer who undertakes the movement of the physical body.

In that context, however, the cognition associated with the word "I" directed toward the body is merely figurative (*lākṣaṇika*). Likewise, in the notion "my self," the sense of "mine-ness" (*mamakāra*) directed toward the body is also merely figurative.
Let it be that "consciousness" (cetana) is intended there; in that case, our term [ātman] is primary. And the body is not consciousness.
For consciousness manifests as inhering in some entity other than the body.
Now, if consciousness is indeed an attribute of the self (*ātman*),
then how is it differentiated with respect to each object when it does not actually come into contact with those objects?
It is said: consciousness (*citi*), which is established by its own manifestation, indeed inheres in the conscious subject (*cetana*).

Furthermore, in the perception of the future and the past, its non-dependence on objects is quite evident. As for the differentiation of consciousness according to each specific object, it is due to the nature of consciousness being such that it conforms to worldly transactional usage (*vyavahāra*).
Since this [consciousness] is designated as belonging to that consciousness which conforms to worldly convention,
there is nothing deficient in this.
The presentation of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).

[Objection: But if, in this way, the distinction from the body were established even at the first sight, then the presentation of recognition—namely, "Having seen this on one day, I saw it again on another day"—would be purposeless.
[Reply: It is said: Even though the distinction is established, [the recognition is presented] in order to establish that [the self] possesses activity by virtue of its stability.
Recognition has been put forward [as a proof].

For if [the self] were unstable, the occasional production of effects would be established by that very fact; therefore, for the sake of establishing that [self], the inference from action does not apply.
The agency and enjoyership of that which is inactive would be merely conceptual;
for the agent and the enjoyer, implied by the statement regarding the sacrificial implements, must be established as real.
The presentation of recognition is appropriate;
for when this self is recognized, then that which is the conscious self (cidātman) possesses its attribute.
That [effect] could never arise from that alone;
for an effect whose cause is always present would not be occasional. Indeed, the delay in the arising of an effect is necessarily dependent upon the non-presence of its cause.

Therefore, this self, being the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), requires some other non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). Regarding this, some say that another operation characterized by cognition, which inheres in that [self], is the non-inherent cause; however, we consider that to be untenable.
Since even that [pleasure] must have some non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) sought for it,
it is better that this belong to consciousness alone;
and that is what is called the contact between the self and the mind (ātma-manas-sannikarṣa).
And its non-inherent cause is the vibration of the mind itself;
for that [vibration] as well, the non-inherent cause is either a distinct contact between the self and the mind accompanied by an effort inherent in the self, or else the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).
Furthermore, between effort and the unseen force (adṛṣṭa), there is indeed another contact between the self and the mind;
this beginningless succession of cause and effect should be understood as being like that of a seed and its sprout. This concludes the presentation of the proof for the acceptance of the mind.
Furthermore, the proof for the acceptance of the mind (*manas*) is precisely the arising of all the qualities of the self;

for all nine specific qualities of the self—namely, cognition (*buddhi*), pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), and mental impression (*saṃskāra*)—arise solely through the conjunction of the self and the mind.
Among these, cognition, which consists of valid knowledge and recollection, is established by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).
Pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort, however, are cognizable through mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*).
Furthermore, pleasure is not merely the absence of pain;
for the absence of pain is of the nature of the non-perception of pleasure.
Because the perception of a self dissociated from that [suffering] is itself of the nature of the non-perception of suffering,
and because there is also the perception of pleasure distinct from the perception of the self;
whereas for the formative force (*saṃskāra*), its effect characterized by memory alone is the indicator.

Since memory occurs only with respect to an object previously experienced, one postulates some excellence (*atiśaya*) of the self dependent upon that experience. However, the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), characterized as merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), is cognizable solely through scripture.
Furthermore, the apprehension of color and other qualities does not arise from the mere contact of the self and the mind alone.
Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of the blind and so forth," the external sense faculties such as the eye are accepted;
and because the effects characterized by the apprehension of external objects such as form are established in five ways, the five [faculties] beginning with the eye are postulated.
That in which the six sense-faculties, beginning with the mind, are supported is the "abode of the faculties," namely, the body.
This is the determination of the threefold nature of the body.
And there is the refutation of the body born from sprouts (*udbhijja*).
That [body] is of three kinds, divided into the womb-born (*jarāyuja*), the egg-born (*aṇḍaja*), and the moisture-born (*saṃsvedaja*);
however, a body born from sprouts does not exist at all.
For that [corpse] is the basis for that [tree], since there is no evidence that trees and the like possess sense-faculties as their bases; [as it is said:
"In a cemetery a tree grows, frequented by herons and vultures."
Thus, because of the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) that the performance of prohibited acts results in such a fruit, it appears that the body is born from a sprout (*udbhijja*).
But even that is untenable,
because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that particular point.
Since tradition (smṛti) lacks a foundation, it is impossible for it to have a primary sense;
nor can the Veda itself be conceived as its source,
because [the Veda] does not have action as its subject matter.
Regarding the rule of the negative particle (*nañvidhi*), there is no lack of intelligibility in the sense that "transgression (*pratyavāya*) results from the performance of what is prohibited.

Although, upon examining the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the *Śaṃyu-adhikaraṇa* (Mīmāṃsā-darśana 3.4.10), it is established that transgression may arise even from something merely prohibited, nevertheless, it cannot be determined that the fruit [of such an act] takes the form of a body consisting of trees and the like.
Because it is unfit for logical concomitance (*anvaya*) by virtue of being a result; for only that whose fitness for concomitance has been ascertained can enter into the meaning of the sentence.
But for that [word] which lacks the possibility of being logically connected with the context,
there is no entry into the meaning of the sentence either,
just as in the case of "one should sprinkle with fire."
As for that usage in the Veda which refers to an object as it actually exists, that must be described as either figurative (gauṇa) or indicative (lākṣaṇika).
In this case as well, it must be described through either a metaphorical (gauṇī) or an indicative (lakṣaṇā) function;
therefore, the body is indeed of three kinds.
Furthermore, as for the body that is asserted by some to be non-earthen (*apārthiva*) and not born from a womb (*ayonija*), being based solely on the sovereign power of merit (*dharma*),
it cannot be inferred because all bodies invariably possess the nature of earth (*pārthivatva*). [This concludes] the examination of the mind (*manas*).
In all bodies, the mind and the skin are two indistinguishable sense-faculties; furthermore,
the mind is within the body and has the dimension of an atom.
That indeed is accepted as being a substance because it possesses the quality of conjunction;
and substance is of two kinds: that which consists of multiple substances and that which is a substance not composed of other substances.
In that regard, if the mind were composed of multiple substances, there would be the conceptual complexity of postulating both the originated and the originating substances; furthermore,
even if it were a substance not composed of other substances, the postulation of its being infinitely large would make conjunction with the self impossible.
For indeed, the conjunction of two things that are infinitely large, devoid of motion, and partless is not possible.
Conjunction is indeed of three kinds: that produced by the action of one, that produced by the action of both,
and that produced by conjunction.
Therefore, the mind has the size of an atom (paramāṇu); and because it exists without a cause, it is eternal. It moves with extreme rapidity.
This is because we observe the extremely rapid functioning of the sense faculties;
for a sense faculty not presided over by that [mind] is not capable of determining its own object,
since one whose mind is distracted elsewhere does not perceive other objects.
The conjunction of that mind with the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) is beginningless and depends upon merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*).

Furthermore, the conjunction with another body occurs through the influence of action (*karman*) produced from the contact between the self and the mind, which itself depends upon the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).
This very self is the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*).
The locus of enjoyment is the body;
the means of enjoyment are the sense organs;
and the objects of enjoyment are internal, such as pleasure and so forth.
The external elements, beginning with earth, and experience— which is consciousness, the feeling of pleasure and pain— are such that all reality is fully encompassed within these five categories.

The determination of the means of valid cognition regarding the self: By what means of valid cognition, then, is this self cognized? For if it were not being cognized, its admission of existence would be without foundation.
Regarding this, some say: "Mental perception is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to the self, just as it is with respect to pleasure and so forth.
The Prābhākaras maintain that this is incorrect;
for one and the same entity cannot simultaneously possess the status of both agent (*kartṛ*) and object (*karma*).
And the status of being an object (karmatva) is established in relation to itself, because it is contradictory for an action to operate upon its own self;
nor can this contradiction be avoided by virtue of the cognition "I am."
This is because its existence is established either by way of self-luminosity or by being the object of the cognition of the [external] object;
and it is only when this is the case that the rule of the simultaneous apprehension of the object and the cognition is logically accounted for.

Others think as follows: indeed, a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is required for objects whose nature is non-luminous so that they may become self-luminous; however, in the case of one's own self, which has luminosity as its very essence, the requirement for luminosity is entirely futile, just as in the case of consciousness itself (saṃvitti).
An Examination of the Self-Luminosity of Consciousness:
Since consciousness is the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it must necessarily be admitted to be self-luminous.
Otherwise, even if it has arisen, if it were not manifest, there would be no linguistic convention regarding the "known-ness" of objects, as their known-ness could not be communicated.

Nor should it be said that for a person, cognition regarding objects is merely their fitness for practical activity (*vyavahāra-yogyatā*), and that this [fitness] is inferred from the result once the activity has arisen;
for it is universally acknowledged by all people that the knownness (*viditatva*) of objects is recognized even prior to the engagement in practical activity.
Nor is consciousness to be apprehended by mental perception;
for while its self-luminosity is established,
there is no evidence for postulating that [mental perception].
For if objects were admitted to be self-luminous and enduring, the states of sleep and so forth would be impossible for persons;
however, this defect does not arise if consciousness is self-luminous, because in states such as sleep, that [consciousness] itself is non-existent.
However, it cannot be asserted that objects— which have acquired their stability through the power of recognition— do not exist for persons even during states such as sleep;
therefore, they depend on something else for their manifestation,
whereas consciousness itself is self-luminous.
The example is established:
the admission of the existence of that which is self-luminous does not depend on another means of valid cognition.
And thus, even in the fourth state, luminosity does not cease.
For this very reason, liberation would not be desired by persons;
even this [position] is declared to be incorrect by those ranked foremost among the authoritative (prāmāṇika).
For if the person were self-luminous, it would follow that there is manifestation even in deep sleep, just as there is in the waking, dreaming, and fourth states.
Self-sleep would not be distinct from them;
for neither the destruction nor the obscuration of that which is inherent is possible.
As for what has been asserted by someone— that even the natural blackness of earth-atoms is removed by contact with fire, which is denoted by the term "cooking"—
that is incorrect;
for whatever is uncreated is entirely indestructible, like space and so forth.

Furthermore, the claim that the blackness of earth-atoms is unproduced is not worthy of respect, as it is sublated by inference; for the natural occurrence of blackness in earth-atoms is not established,
since, like redness, it is admitted to be produced by heating (*pākaja*).
Eternity is simply the state of being without a cause.
If that which is causeless were also impermanent, then no definition of eternity would be possible.
The exposition of our own view:
Those who know reality declare that it is established that the self does not appear unpermeated by objects, nor do objects appear when the cognizer is not manifest.
In that regard, whatever validity there is concerning objects,
the consciousness produced by it arises manifesting both the person and its own objects as its content.
Even though the person (puruṣa) partakes in the fruit of that cognition, he does not possess the status of an object (karmatā),

but rather the status of an agent (kartṛtā) alone, just like a goer. For example, although a goer is connected with the conjunction that is the fruit of the act of going, he does not possess the status of an object.
But just as agency itself [is to be understood], so too should the state of being a knower be understood;
for those who know the nature of action define "object" (karman) as that which is connected with an action and its result inherent in another.
For this very reason, the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*) is also established for the object, the knower, and the self-awareness.

And thus, because the Self is the object of the cognition of the object, it is entirely logical that it does not manifest during sleep and other such states, due to the cessation of the means for the perception of objects.
Even in the fourth state (*turīya*), the Self, though possessing all possible means of apprehension, remains in the state of pure existence (*sanmātra*) alone.
The description of one's own view is that liberation is simply the cessation of suffering;
nor is liberation a non-goal for man,
because liberation consists in the coming to rest of the manifold sufferings of saṃsāra.
For the cessation of suffering is indeed sought by persons.

And this is not tenable: that just as it possesses the status of the supreme human goal because it consists in the cessation of all suffering, so too it would lack the status of a human goal because it consists in the annihilation of all happiness.

Since the wise consider worldly happiness— because it is dependent on external means and characterized by perishability— to be nothing but suffering swallowed by pain, they do not cherish it excessively;
for this very reason, they exert themselves for the sake of liberation.
And thus, even the acceptance of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*) is of little fruit; nor can it be established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
because the Vedas lack the capacity to convey an already established entity.
Furthermore, there is a contradiction with direct perception;
those who are transmigrating do not experience such bliss.
Nor is it the case that they do not experience it because it has been overcome.
Because it is impossible for an intrinsic, self-luminous bliss to be suppressed;
nor is the nature of the Self as bliss established by its being the object of supreme love,
since love for the Self is not established.
For since suffering arises from the injury of the body, everyone seeks to avoid such injury; thus, there is a conceit of love for the self.
Furthermore, since the natural supreme bliss of transmigrating beings has never been experienced before, how could there be love for the self based upon that?
Therefore, it is elegant [to say] that bliss (*ānanda*) arises solely from the enjoyment of specific objects;
furthermore, liberation (*mokṣa*) is a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) because it is the cessation of the suffering of saṃsāra—
this is the restatement of the view of Maṇḍanamiśra.
But what is this liberation? Some say it is the cessation of ignorance.
It is the reality of Brahman, which is one alone, without a second, unconditioned, and purified of all limiting adjuncts.

Thus, by the power of beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*), that which appears as if accompanied by a body and other such things, as if defiled by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), and having acquired the designation "living being" (*jīva*),
is perceived as if bound. Therefore, beginningless ignorance itself is *saṃsāra*.
"Liberation is simply the setting of that [ignorance] due to the arising of perfectly pure knowledge that transcends all conceptual construction"—
this is refuted:
those who rely on valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) consider this to be merely a manifestation of blind faith.
This might be so if non-duality were within the scope of some means of valid cognition;
but it is not thus,
for non-duality is certainly not within the scope of any means of valid cognition.
It might be thought: "Perception itself, its operation exhausted by mere affirmation, directly realizes a single, non-dual reality that is untouched by mutual differentiation.
That is incorrect—while it is true that perception is indeed affirmative, even while affirming, it [affirms] form as form, [color as color], and so forth.
It establishes taste as being of the nature of taste,
yet not everything [is reduced] to oneness,
just as there is a continuous stream of cognition regarding form.
If it were indeed such [an entity] even in the case of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*),
then non-duality would certainly be directly realized through perception;
however, this is not the case, as is self-evident to the consciousness of every cognizer.
Furthermore, having established through the conceptualization of the object of cognition that the entity is merely a universal,
and having proven that existence is nothing more than that because existence is the nature of the "great universal" (mahāsāmānya),
that too is like attempting to swallow the sky.
Being (*sattva*) is not merely a particular entity, because it exists everywhere;
for it is impossible to deny the universal (*sāmānya*), which is cognized as appearing in all occurrences.
Nor is there a single entity whose nature consists of both the universal and the particular.
Because it is contradictory for a single entity to possess two forms, perception apprehends two distinct entities—namely, the universal and the particular—which are mutually connected;
thus, how could the proof of a dual nature (sattādvaita) be established?
Furthermore, as in this case, there is no cognition of both the universal and the particular, or the genus and the individual, occurring simultaneously.
Likewise, it has been determined in the *Jātinirṇaya*, page 50 [of the Prajñāprakāśa]:
"Nor is non-duality established through scripture alone;
that is not so."
Because scripture has as its sole object that which is to be accomplished (*kārya*), it cannot be established as authoritative with respect to an already established reality (*siddha*).
Furthermore, scripture is held to be authoritative as consisting of sentences;
and such a sentence, being composed of multiple words, generates a cognition regarding the meaning of the sentence, which consists of the meanings of those multiple words.
How could non-duality (advaita) manifest?

To this it is replied: "This is the instruction: 'Not this, not this'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26). By the negation of all limiting adjuncts (upādhi), other diverse entities are excluded, and thus non-duality is established through scripture (āgama).

That too is without substance: for that object which is indeed apprehended as having the nature of existence (*sat*) is unfit to be connected with the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), which brings about non-existence.
It is like the case of "it exists" and "it does not exist.
Furthermore, because it is impossible for two word-meanings that are incapable of being related to undergo such a relation, they cannot constitute the meaning of a sentence.
If this is so, then all negative sentences would be utterly refuted.
O dull-witted one, do not think thus;
for in prohibitive statements there is no absolute negation of anything whatsoever, but rather something specific is negated in a particular context.
But you, who hold the conceit of the non-duality of Brahman, desire an absolute negation.
And thus, this very arrow of your own strikes you: "When something has acquired a form in some respect, only that which is similar to it can be negated;
therefore, without a prior affirmation, a negation is impossible."
[Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Śaṅkara Bhāṣya, Kāṇḍa 1, Adhyāya 4, Brāhmaṇa 10, Śloka 2].

Therefore, because its meaning contradicts perception and other means of valid cognition, it is not logical to explain the scripture that teaches non-duality (advaita) according to its literal sense. As for this which has been established through detailed argumentation—that even in the face of contradiction with perception and other means, the scripture alone possesses superior authority—[it is as follows:]
On that basis, one might suppose that it is perception and the other means of knowledge themselves that must be considered erroneous;
however, that too is a mere wishful thought.

This is because when there is a contradiction with perception and the rest, words lack the capacity for their meanings to cohere, and thus no understanding of meaning can arise from scripture when it contradicts them.
Therefore, because it contradicts perception and other means of valid cognition, one must resort to a figurative or metaphorical interpretation of the scripture;
this is the explanation of the scriptural passages concerning bliss and so forth according to our own view.
In this regard, scriptural passages concerning bliss (*ānanda*) and so forth should be explained as referring to the natural absence of suffering;
they must be interpreted as such because worldly bliss is limited and invariably accompanied by suffering.
And the scriptural passages concerning oneness are intended to show that within a single locus, there is the sovereignty of only one [Self].
As it is said, "Indra moves in many forms through his powers of illusion" (māyābhiḥ);
the meaning is that, due to the conceit of identifying the body as the Self, he appears as if divided in birth after birth.

The meaning of the negation of plurality is that even when assuming many bodies, the Self is one and the same. Furthermore, the passage "This is not this, not this" is intended to establish what is distinct from the body and so forth by negating their status as the Self. And the scriptural texts concerning consciousness are intended to express the distinction [of the Self] from ether and other elements due to its possession of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*).

Furthermore, all scriptural passages concerning the "Self of all" are figurative expressions based on the fact that everything exists for the sake of the Self; as it is said in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (4.5.6) and the Maitrāyaṇī Brāhmaṇa: "When the Self is known, all this becomes known.
This is because the knowledge of the Self has liberation as its fruit, which is the supreme goal of human existence.
This is the general direction [of the argument]: to show that once that [Self] is known, all other knowledge is entirely fruitless.

Now, it might be argued: "The manifestation of anything distinct from consciousness that is not itself of the nature of light is logically impossible. Whatever manifests, [must be so by virtue of consciousness].
Each of those [objects] is non-different from the Light,
and Brahman is of the nature of Light;
therefore, it is established that the world has Brahman as its self, and thus non-duality (advaita) is proven.
921. This contradicts your own position. How can the wise assert such a thing?

For if there were no distinction in the manifestation (*prakāśa*) of various forms (*ākāra*), then the manifestation itself would necessarily become manifold; thus, non-duality (*advaita*) would be utterly discarded.
Now, it might be argued: "This manifold proliferation of forms appears due to the power of the superimposition of ignorance (*avidyādhyāsa*).
This too is self-contradictory;
for [according to you], luminosity is of the nature of existence (*sadātman*).
Therefore, it is not tenable that the forms, which are non-different from the self that is non-luminous, are themselves luminous; for if that were the case, how could they possibly manifest?
Furthermore, it has been stated in the *Bāhyārthasiddhi* that manifestation is possible only for that which is inherently non-luminous.
Therefore, this too is merely the delusion of the proponents of Brahman, as it involves entering the position of the Mahāyānists.
Furthermore, how could ignorance possibly manifest a conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) that is absolutely non-existent?
Indeed, ignorance is not the manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*).
However, it has been established in the *Nayavīthī* that [ignorance] consists solely in the form of non-apprehension;
therefore, liberation is not the cessation of ignorance.
[Here follows] the definition of liberation and its means according to our own school's view.

However, it is logical that liberation is the absolute severance of the body, based upon the complete exhaustion of all merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*). For it is under the influence of merit and demerit that the living soul (*jīva*) transmigrates through various states of existence (*yoni*).

When those two [merit and demerit] are completely annihilated, one who is divested from the connection with body and sense-faculties and has uprooted the entire succession of worldly suffering is said to be liberated.
But how, then, is there the total exhaustion of all dharma and adharma?
It is certainly not by means of experience alone.

Because it is impossible to exhaust the infinite accumulations of *karmāśayas*— those gathered throughout the beginningless continuum of the body, as well as those being accumulated even at the time of experiencing their fruits—

it is said: "Indeed, he who is distressed by the sufferings of *saṃsāra*, and who, having become free from desire even for pleasures tainted by their association with suffering, exerts himself for the sake of liberation (*mokṣa*)," [is the one capable of such exhaustion].

Turning away from those prohibited acts which are causes of bondage and those which cause demerit (pratyavāya), as well as from optional rites (kāmya) which are means to worldly prosperity (abhyudaya), he brings to exhaustion through experience the previously accumulated merit and demerit; then, by means of self-knowledge— strengthened by its auxiliaries such as tranquility (śama), self-control (dama), and celibacy (brahmacarya)— and impelled toward non-return according to the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (8.15.1), "He does not return again," he destroys the entire latent residue of karma (karmāśaya).
One is liberated;
nor is this description of non-returning merely an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda),
because the knowledge of the Self serves no other purpose.

For if it were for the sake of another, the mention of the fruit in the case of the *parṇamayī* [vessel] would be explained as a mere explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*) according to the established principle; however,

since the injunction of knowledge is not for the sake of another, that very [mention of the fruit] serves as a qualification of the person entitled to perform the act, as in the case of the *rātrisatra*.
Furthermore, the knowledge of the self is not a subordinate part of the injunctions for ritual action, because it is not for the sake of another,
and there is no evidence for its being for the sake of another.
The determination of the size of the self according to our own view:
Now, what is the proof for the liberated self’s abiding as pure existence alone, beyond all perception? It is said: That which is existent and without cause...
That [self] is indestructible like the sky;
and the dimension of the self is supreme magnitude, like the sky. Wherever a quality of the self is perceived, [there the self exists].
In each respective case, it is established by valid means of knowledge that the self exists there, because a quality cannot exist without its possessor.
Regarding this matter, however, there is this doubt: does it approach [the body] by moving? Or...
Or [it may be] independent of motion; in that case,
if one relies on its dependence upon motion, there must first be the postulation of motion, and for that [motion], a non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) must be postulated.

And there is no means of valid cognition for that [existence], because proximity is possible even for one who is not moving, just as in the case of space. Now, it might be argued: "Even where the body does not exist..."
If the self were present there as well, then its qualities would be perceived there just as they are in the body;
but that is not the case.
Since the contact between the self and the mind is the non-inherent cause of all qualities of the self,
and since that conjunction, by virtue of residing in two loci, cannot exist elsewhere in the absence of the mind,
and it has been stated that the mind resides within the body.
And since the effect occurs precisely where the non-inherent cause is located, qualities are not perceived outside of the self.
[Objection: But in that case, the postulation of motion for the body would likewise be without any means of valid cognition (apramāṇaka). [Reply: No.
Because it would follow that something existing in one place could be perceived elsewhere;

however, since it is impossible to attribute the consequence of being perceived to the self—even though it exists—on the grounds that it transcends the path of all sensory organs, the self must necessarily be conjoined with all things possessed of conjunction.
And since this [conjunction] is not possible without its being of infinite magnitude, it is not of atomic dimension.
Or [the soul] has the same dimensions as the body.
And having the same dimensions as the body is untenable without possessing parts (*sāvayavatva*).
For such magnitude depends on one or another of the following: a multiplicity of parts, magnitude itself, or a specific kind of accumulation (*pracaya*).
Furthermore, the postulation of parts is not supported by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
[Objection: But if the *puruṣa* were omnipresent, would it not follow that experience (*bhoga*) would occur even in other bodies?
[Reply: Not so.
Whatever body belongs to someone, that is the locus for the enjoyment of its experiences; and whatever sense-faculties belong to someone, [those are likewise].
Since those [faculties] are the instruments of his enjoyment,
there is no consequence of enjoyment occurring in another locus. This concludes the resolution of the doubt regarding the confusion of enjoyments if the self were all-pervasive.
Now, one might ask: what is the basis for the specific determination of the connection between the body and the sense organs?
It is said in reply: you should understand that it is based on the connection with merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*).
For those bodies and sense organs which have been acquired by means of specific instances of merit and demerit, [the connection is determined accordingly].
"These [objects] are the means of enjoyment for that very [self].

If it is asked, "Upon what does the determination of dharma and adharma depend?"—the determination of the connection with karma is based on the connection with the body and sense organs, which serve as its inherent causes (samavāyikāraṇa). Thus, because the continuum of bodies, sense organs, dharma, and adharma is beginningless, everything is logically consistent.
In the refutation of the doubt regarding the oneness of the self.
If the self possesses omnipresence (*vibhutva*), then let there be only one single self in all bodies, just like the sky. For example,
the sky is indeed one, yet it relates to various individual objects such as jars, water-pots, and so forth.
In that case, why is a self (*ātman*) not likewise accepted?
Why is there the acceptance of a distinction for each sense-base (*āyatana*)?

It is said: First, the cognizer perceives through inference—by means of observing an activity similar to his own, which is produced by his own effort and inherent in his own body—the owner of another's body as being possessed of effort.
It is not [perceived] as having the single flavor of the subject (*grāhaka*),
but rather as being non-self (*anātman*) and situated within the category of the object (*grāhya*).
For that reason, since the difference [between subject and object] is established by cognition, [the object is indeed distinct].
The statement, "Enough with the admission of difference," is ineffective;

for an inference such as "it belongs to the owner of another's body" cannot possibly arise. Just as [one infers] regarding my own body that its movement is preceded by my own effort, [so too must it be in other cases].
Likewise, [the claim] that even in another's body [volitional effort] is based solely on my own effort is contradicted by perception;
for by perception, volitional effort is apprehended as inhering in one's own self.
And indeed, a volitional effort conducive to the movements of another's body is not perceived within one's own self by persons.
Effort belongs only to another [person], yet it is inferred in the body of another.
Now, if the self of another is thus perceived through inference, how can this be said: “He is ungraspable, for he is not grasped” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.2.4)?

It is said that this statement—"it is not perceived by another"—has this intended meaning: "it is not perceived by another because it consists of a single essence as the grasper"; such is its meaning, and therefore there is no contradiction.
Furthermore, persons are distinct and manifold according to each body, because we observe the distinct arrangements of merit and demerit, pleasure and pain, and so forth.
Otherwise, indeed, dharma, adharma, and so forth would belong to one person for everyone.
This is the doubt raised according to the opinion of the author of the *Brahmasiddhi*.
Here, a certain person who considers himself wise says: "The distinction between pleasure, pain, and so forth will be merely conceptual (*kālpānika*)."
Just as within a single body the distribution of sensations in the feet and other parts does not overlap, so too it will not overlap across various bodies;
for a sensation occurring in the foot does not occur in the head.
Nor is it the case that a sensation located in the head is present in the foot;
nor can it be said that a sensation inheres only in the feet and so forth,
because those [limbs] are insentient.
For the knower is indeed bound together with the feelings,
because they consist of specific forms of suffering;
this is the refutation of that [position].
"This is merely a delusion of foolish people," say the elders. "I have pain in my foot."
"In my head there is pain"—thus, among all sensations, one person manifests as suffering.
However, in the feet and other parts, one experiences heat and so forth. In that context, "heat" (*santāpa*) is the conjunction with fire (*tejas*).
Furthermore, whether it be pain from a stake or that which arises from the agitation of wind, bile, and phlegm, this should be understood to apply to all disorders.
Even in the case of insentient objects such as a foot [being pierced], there is no contradiction in its contact with bile and the other humors;
the suffering produced by that [contact] inheres in the self alone.

Now, it might be argued: just as the state of being a reflection belongs to a single object—the original—due to the influence of limiting conditions such as a gem, a sword, or a mirror, and just as properties such as blackness are distributed accordingly;
so too, due to the influence of various bodies as limiting conditions, pleasure and other states are distributed to a single self.

That is incorrect—because qualities such as blackness, which are adventitious (*aupādhika*), are subject to their respective limiting conditions (*upādhi*) and thus lack a connection with the original object (*bimba*).
Therefore, this systematic distinction is possible only for those properties that exist within a single substratum (*ekadharmin*).
Pleasure and the like, however, are not adventitious.

However, since these [qualities] would inhere only in the self, their systematic arrangement as residing in a single self would be untenable. Furthermore, this conceptual construction might be possible if the oneness of the self were established;
yet, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the oneness of the self.
Furthermore, the scriptural authorities concerning the single soul have already had their meaning explained;
thus, it is established that the persons in each body are distinct.
In this manner, Śālikānātha has set forth the *Tattvāloka*.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Illumination of Reality" (*Tattvāloka*), in the *Prakaraṇapañcikā* composed by the Great Professor (*Mahāmahopādhyāya*) Śrī Śālikanātha Miśra.
